name: Building AI Agents with LangGraph | Abhinav Ralhan
snippet: Building AI Agents with LangGraph | Abhinav Ralhan # Building AI Agents with LangGraph The term “AI agent” gets thrown around loosely. At its core, an agent is an LLM that can decide what actions to take, execute them, observe the results, and decide what to do next. The key distinction from a chain is the loop — the LLM reasons iteratively rather than following a fixed sequence. LangGraph makes this loop explicit by modeling agents as graphs with nodes, edges, and state. This post covers when and how to use it. - The LangGraph models agents as directed graphs: This creates the core agent loop: Agent reasons → calls tool → observes result → reasons again → eventually returns. Tools are the agent’s interface to external systems. Well-designed tools make the agent more reliable; poorly designed tools cause confusion and wasted iterations. Too many tools: An agent with 20 tools performs worse than one with 5. The LLM has to reason about which tool to use, and more options means more confusion. Group related functionality into fewer, broader tools. Vague tool descriptions: “Query the database” is unhelpful. “Query daily API usage metrics for a specific account, returning call counts, error rates, and trends” helps the LLM understand when to use it. Tools that require multi-step reasoning: If a tool needs three parameters that must be gathered from other tools first, the agent has to plan a sequence. Simpler tools that take one obvious parameter are more reliable. ## LangGraph vs LangChain Agents LangChain has its ownAgentExecutor that also implements the ReAct loop. Why use LangGraph instead? | Aspect | LangChain AgentExecutor | LangGraph | | --- | --- | --- | | Control flow | Implicit loop | Explicit graph | | Customization | Limited hooks | Full control over nodes/edges | | Debugging | Trace through loop iterations | Visualize graph, inspect state | | Human-in-the-loop | Callbacks | Native interrupt/resume | | Multi-agent | Not built-in | First-class support | | State | Message history only | Custom state with reducers | LangGraph is the direction the LangChain ecosystem is moving. For new projects, default to LangGraph. An alternative to a plan, executes each step: This pattern works better for complex, multi-step tasks because the LLM considers the full approach upfront rather than making one-step-at-a-time decisions. The downside is higher latency (extra LLM call for planning) and rigidity (the plan may not adapt well to unexpected results). - ReAct: Exploratory queries, variable-length investigations, conversational agents - Plan-and-Execute: Well-defined workflows, multi-step procedures, report generation Production agents need constraints: - Max iterations: Cap the ReAct loop (e.g., 10 tool calls max) to prevent runaway costs - Tool call validation: Validate parameters before executing (e.g., SQL injection prevention) - Output validation: Use Pydantic models to enforce structured output - Cost tracking: Log token usage per invocation, set budget limits - Timeout: Kill agent runs that exceed time limits - Fallback: If the agent fails, return a graceful error rather than crashing ## Practical Takeaways - Default to chains for predictable workflows. Only use agents when the LLM needs to decide what to do next - Keep the tool count low (3-5 tools) with clear, specific docstrings - Use LangGraph over LangChain’s AgentExecutor for new projects — the explicit graph is easier to debug and extend - Always set iteration limits — agents without guardrails will burn through your API budget - Test agents with diverse queries, not just the happy path — edge cases reveal tool design problems - Start with ReAct for general-purpose agents, Plan-and-Execute for structured workflows
